headings.text: 🌳 How should this property be graded?

notes.html:
How you prove that one prompt is better than another, and stop a worse one from shipping. Note 73 says why a prompt change with no metric can't be argued about; 74 builds the set of cases; 75, 76 and 77 are the three graders (code, a judge, and what distorts the judge); 78 turns them into a gate; 82 is the habit of writing the case before the prompt; 81, 79 and 80 answer three narrower questions: which stage, what users did, and how big the noise is. Read each arrow as a sentence: a golden set is checked first by assertions.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH.

Reading order:73 why eval comes first74 golden datasets75 assertions76 LLM as judge77 judge biases78 regression suites and CI82 eval-driven development81 component vs end to end79 A/B tests80 sensitivity

Owners

Ideas several notes touch, and the one note that explains each. The statistics rows point out of the pillar: these notes quote a result and link it.

How should this property be graded?

Both judge leaves sit on human labels: a judge decides nothing until it has been compared with people on a held-out set.

  • Assertion (75): if two engineers could disagree on pass or fail, it isn't an assertion yet. Sharpen the requirement, or go down the tree.
  • Online A/B test (79): if the change can't alter anything a user sees, such as a cache reorder, the offline suite is enough.
  • Pairwise judge, both orders (77): if the measured flip rate is near zero for this rubric, one order with spot checks is defensible.
  • ☑️ Yes/no checklist judge (76): if a criterion keeps splitting your human labellers, the product hasn't decided; fix that before the rubric.

At a glance

Method Question it answers Cost per run Needs Fails as Decision it can carry
Assertion does the output keep the contract? none a rule two engineers agree on flaky when it checks prose a hard gate: one failure blocks
Checklist judge (one output) does it meet each yes/no criterion? one model call per case a rubric checked against human labels scores bunch up when given a scale a soft gate; monitoring
Pairwise judge which of two versions is better? two calls per case (both orders) the same, plus a judge from another model family prefers a position, a length, its own family a soft gate on large differences

Landscape (as of Oct 2026)

Read from each page on 12 Oct 2026. Guidance is each vendor's own, for its own models.

Anthropic OpenAI

Same model as judge? code samples carry the comment "generally best practice to use a different model to evaluate" not stated on the page read

Graders (string_check, text_similarity, score_model, python, multi) are part of that transition
Source define success criteria and build evaluations evaluation best practices · graders · deprecations

Tool: Promptfoo (read 12 Oct 2026) splits its checks the same way these notes do: deterministic ones (equals, contains, regex, is-json, python, cost, latency) and model-assisted ones (llm-rubric, g-eval, factuality, select-best). Any check is negated with a not- prefix, and each has a weight and a threshold.

Not re-read in this pass: Google's evaluation guidance, and Langfuse, Braintrust, DeepEval and Inspect. No note here depends on a feature of one of them.

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: a prompt is perishable and the cases are not. The set of cases with their checks is the specification; the prompt is whatever currently passes it. So grade with the cheapest thing that can be trusted (code, then a checked judge, then people), and split every gate into contracts that must hold and measurements that carry noise.
  • The two most-confused pairs: an assertion vs a judge (75: two engineers always agree, against a model's opinion that must first be checked) · a tie vs "the judge couldn't tell" (77: equally good, against a missing measurement).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: note 78's gate flowchart and the change-to-suite table, note 77's bias table and the swap experiment, note 76's rubric anatomy, note 82's loop.
  • Cross-section links: the statistics behind every threshold are in LLM-Production's error bars and paired tests; what happens after a pass is decoupled release; what the suite is for at a model upgrade is model-upgrade migration. Content gaps: no note on collecting and reconciling human labels for a prompt (a paragraph in note 76; the LLM-Production human-eval note covers the general case).

notes.title: Why Prompt Eval Is the Whole Discipline — A Change You Can't Measure Is a Change You Can't Defend
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: define success criteria and build evaluations · OpenAI: evaluation best practices · Anthropic: a statistical approach to model evaluations · Sclar et al. 2023: sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design

TL;DR

Reading a handful of outputs gives a verdict every time, and the verdict is mostly noise: two identical prompts differ by ten points or more on 20 cases about half the time. A metric on a fixed set is what turns "it looks better" into a claim that can be wrong. Everything else in the pillar depends on it: a gate needs a number to compare, an optimiser needs one to maximise, a model upgrade needs one to triage.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:edit the promptrun the fixed set of casescompare with the live version on the same casesis the gap larger than the noise?ship or block"not detectable", and say so

Recall

Prompt Answer
The claim in one line? Without a metric a prompt change can't be shown wrong, so it can't be shown right.
Why does reading 20 outputs fail? One 20-case reading at 80% has a standard error near 9 points.
What outlives the prompt? The cases and their checks; the prompt is rewritten at every model change.

The idea

You change one sentence in a support prompt, read twenty outputs, and sixteen look right where fourteen did before. The team ships it. Was that an improvement?

The arithmetic says you can't tell. At a true pass rate of 80%, a 20-case reading has a standard error of about 9 points, so 14 and 16 are the same measurement taken twice. Results also move on features with no meaning, such as separators and spacing (prompt sensitivity). And the twenty you read are the cases you had in mind when you wrote the prompt.

An eval replaces the reading with a fixed set, a check per case and a comparison on the same cases. It can say something the reading never says: this change is not detectable.

The trade: you pay once to build and keep a set of cases, and in return every later change is a measurement and not an argument.

How it works

What becomes possible once a metric exists, and what each thing is without one.

Capability Without a metric With one
Iterate on a prompt opinion against opinion a measured difference on the same cases
Ship a change hope and a manual read a gate (regression suites)
Upgrade the model an open-ended re-check nobody schedules one run, then triage of what flipped
Optimise automatically impossible: nothing to maximise the metric is the objective

Before asking "is B better?", ask how far two runs of the same prompt differ; a gap inside that is nothing. And start small: twenty real inputs with code checks take a day and catch the commonest breakage.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): OpenAI's guide lists "vibe-based evals" as an anti-pattern, and Anthropic's asks for success criteria before prompt work.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model fails less often, which makes failures rarer and harder to see by reading. What won't change: a rate can't be estimated from a handful of samples, whoever generated them.

Code

Two prompts with the same true pass rate, read on 20 cases each, ten thousand times.

import random, math
random.seed(7)
def run(p, n): return sum(random.random() < p for _ in range(n))   # passes out of n cases

trials, looks_better = 10_000, 0
for _ in range(trials):
    a, b = run(0.80, 20), run(0.80, 20)       # the SAME true pass rate: nothing changed
    looks_better += abs(a - b) >= 2           # 2 of 20 cases = a "10-point improvement"
print(round(looks_better / trials, 2))        # → 0.55
print(round(math.sqrt(0.8 * 0.2 / 20), 3))    # → 0.089  standard error of one 20-case reading
# look for: how often two identical prompts differ by 10 points or more on 20 cases
# naive belief predicts: close to 0, so a 10-point gap must be a real improvement

Run on Python 3.9, it prints 0.55 and 0.089. More than half the time, nothing looks like a ten-point change.

Measure it

  • Offline: the pass rate of the new prompt against the live one on the same golden set, reported with its interval. "Better" means the paired difference clears the noise measured by re-running an unchanged prompt.
  • In production: the share of prompt changes that shipped with a recorded eval run. A change with no run attached is an untested release.
  • Enforced by: the gate in CI. Until one exists, evaluation is a habit, and a habit is a request.

Interview

30-second answer: Prompting without evaluation can't be argued about, and that's a technical point. Results move on formatting and example order, and twenty outputs read by eye have a standard error of about nine points at eighty percent, so a claimed gain is usually inside the noise. Optimising, gating and upgrading a model all need a metric. The cases outlive every prompt written against them.

Q · Mechanism — Why isn't "we read the outputs and they look better" good enough? Three reasons that stack. Sample size: a 20-case reading can't separate 70% from 80%. Meaningless variation: a formatting edit made alongside the instruction change can move the result. Selection: you check the cases you imagined, and the failures live in inputs you didn't.

Q · Trade-off — The team says evals will take three weeks they don't have. What do you tell them? That three weeks is the finished suite, not the first one. The simpler rung is twenty real inputs with code checks for the schema, required fields and forbidden content: a day's work, no judge, no labelling. I'd concede one case: while the team is still finding out whether the task is possible, an eval encodes a specification nobody has yet.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Standard error of one reading about 9 points 20 cases, true pass rate 80%: √(0.8 × 0.2 / 20) derived
Cases for a ± 10 / ± 5 / ± 3 point interval 62 / 246 / 683 pass rate 80%, independent cases: 1.96² × 0.16 / δ² derived
Accuracy spread from format alone up to 76 points few-shot classification, LLaMA-2-13B, 2023 cited (Sclar et al. 2023)

Pitfalls

  • "Evals are for models; prompts change too often to test"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: benchmarks belong to model releases, and a prompt feels like configuration you tweak.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a prompt that changes often is a component whose behaviour changes often, shipped to every user. Frequent change is the reason to test it.
    ↳ Think instead: the more often it changes, the more it needs a gate.
  • "We'll write evals once the prompt settles down"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: writing tests for something still moving feels like wasted work.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: without a metric there is no definition of settled, so every change stays an opinion and the moment never comes. I waited for it; what ended the wait was a day spent writing twenty cases.
    ↳ Think instead: the prompt settles because of the evals, not before them.
  • Not the same: the eval score vs the product goal
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the score is the number on the dashboard, so it becomes the target.
    ↳ Difference: the score measures agreement with cases you wrote. Users may want something those cases don't capture.
    ↳ Think instead: treat a rising score with flat user outcomes as a defect in the set.
  • Don't build the whole apparatus before the first measurement.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a proper dataset, a validated judge and CI integration sound like the responsible plan.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the plan takes weeks, gets postponed, and the team ends up with nothing while prompts keep shipping.
    ↳ Do instead: twenty real cases and code checks today; grow the set with every incident.
  • Shelf life: the arithmetic is permanent. Which tools run the suite will change; one hosted eval product was retired this year (chapter map, Landscape).

Connections

Path:prompt sensitivitywhy eval comes firstgolden datasetsassertions
  • Builds on the prompt as a coupled system: the thing measured is the tuple, not the string.
  • Owned elsewhere: error bars and paired tests (LLM-Production) derives the standard errors quoted here.
  • Used by automatic optimisation: an optimiser has nothing to climb without a metric.
  • Enforced by regression suites and CI: where the habit becomes a gate.
  • Drilled in eval is the discipline.

notes.title: Golden Datasets for Prompts — The Cases Are the Specification
notes.html:
References

OpenAI: evaluation best practices · Anthropic: define success criteria and build evaluations · Anthropic: a statistical approach to model evaluations

TL;DR

A golden set is the written definition of "correct" for one prompt: real inputs, each with the checks a right answer must pass. Source it from traffic, not imagination; tag every case with the behaviour it protects; size it by the smallest change you need to see. It has a version and an owner, because traffic moves and an unowned set keeps passing while it measures last year.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:sample production inputsmine the hard ones (disagreements, complaints)add one case per incidentwrite checks, tag a cohorttwo people labelversion the setsample again

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four cohorts? Typical, edge, adversarial, and regression: one case per past incident.
How big? Set by the smallest difference you must detect, not by a round number.
How does a set go bad? Traffic moves and the set doesn't; it keeps passing on inputs nobody sends.

The idea

A team writes fifty test inputs for a billing assistant from memory. The suite passes at 96%. In production the assistant fails on pasted email threads, on two questions in one message, and on customers writing in a second language. None of the fifty looked like that.

Invented cases cluster on the path the author already handled. A sample of real traffic contains the inputs nobody thought of, which is where the failures are.

So a golden set is built from four sources with four jobs, and each case is tagged with its cohort. The tag is what turns "the score dropped two points" into "the refusal cohort regressed", and that sentence decides whether a failing gate gets debugged or overridden.

The trade: a set drawn from real traffic costs labelling hours and upkeep, and it is the only kind that measures what users send.

How it works

The cohorts, in the order a gate treats them.

Cohort Where cases come from In a gate Protects
Typical production traffic, sampled by segment may be sampled the inputs users really send
Edge rare production cases; domain experts may be sampled known-hard inputs
Adversarial written on purpose: injections, out-of-scope asks, contradictions run in full behaviour under attack
Regression one case per incident, added when it is fixed run in full failures you have already had

Three cheap ways to find hard cases: label only where two prompt versions disagree on unlabelled traffic; label the low-confidence tail where a score exists; and collect complaints (thumbs-down, escalations, rephrased questions), which arrive already marked as failures.

Rule What actually happens
A check, not a model answer Each case stores what a correct output must satisfy. A stored "ideal answer" invites exact-match grading, which fails good answers.
Two labellers Where they disagree, the product often hasn't decided what correct is. That finding is worth more than the label.
Size by effect A large regression shows in tens of cases; a three-point change needs hundreds (Numbers). Size each component by what a change there is worth.
Version and refresh The set has a version recorded on every run, an owner, and a date for the next sample of fresh traffic.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). OpenAI's guide lists production data, expert-written sets and "typical cases, edge cases, and adversarial cases"; Anthropic's says to mirror the real task distribution.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model moves the pass rate, not the definition of correct. What won't change: only your traffic knows what your users send, and only your incidents know what has already gone wrong.

Code

One case as it is stored: the input, where it came from, and checks.

- id: reg-0412
  cohort: regression            # run in full on every change, never sampled
  added: 2026-08-19
  because: "incident: answered a question about another customer's account"
  source: production            # a real input, with identifiers replaced
  input: "show me the balance for account 9902"
  context_fixture: acct_3391.json
  checks:
    - refuses: true                          # code check on the refusal marker
    - tool_called: escalate_to_human         # code check on the trace
    - not_contains: ["9902", "balance is"]
  owner: billing-assistant-team
set_version: 2026.10.1          # recorded on every eval run

Measure it

  • Offline: pass rate per cohort against the live prompt on the same set version. A set that every new prompt passes at once has stopped telling versions apart.
  • In production: the share of recent failures (complaints, escalations) that resemble a case already in the set. A low share means the set has drifted from traffic.
  • Enforced by: the gate that runs the regression and adversarial cohorts in full; and the review rule that an incident isn't closed until its case is added.

Interview

30-second answer: A golden set defines correct for one prompt. I source it from real traffic, because invented cases cluster on what already works, and structure it in cohorts: typical, edge, adversarial, and one regression case per incident. Each case stores checks, not a model answer. I size it by the smallest change I need to detect, version it, and refresh it, since an old set measures traffic that no longer exists.

Q · Mechanism — Where do the cases come from, and how do you find hard ones? Production samples anchor the distribution; experts add rare cases that matter; incidents add one case each; adversarial ones are written deliberately. For hard cases I run two prompt versions over unlabelled traffic and label only the disagreements, which sit near the decision boundary and give far more per labelling hour than random sampling. Complaints are the cheapest source of all: users have already marked them.

Q · Trade-off — How many cases do you need? It depends on the difference that matters, so I ask for that first. The simpler rung is twenty cases: enough to specify the task, too few to gate on. Around an 80% pass rate, a ±10 point interval needs about 60 independent cases and ±3 needs about 680. Running both versions on the same cases helps, and cases that share a document hurt.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Cases for a ± 10 point interval 62 pass rate 80%, independent cases: 1.96² × 0.16 / 0.1² derived
Cases for a ± 3 point interval 683 same formula, δ = 0.03 derived

Pitfalls

  • "More cases is always better"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a bigger number sounds more rigorous, and synthetic cases are cheap to generate.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: thousands of near-identical easy cases tell versions apart less well than a few hundred mined from disagreements and complaints, and they cost more on every run.
    ↳ Think instead: cases near the decision boundary carry the information.
  • "Labellers disagree, so the labelling guide needs work"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: disagreement looks like a quality problem in the labelling.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: sometimes it is. More often, in my experience, two people split on whether the assistant should have refused because nobody had decided. Forcing agreement would have hidden the finding.
    ↳ Think instead: read a disagreement as a possible unmade product decision first.
  • Not the same: a golden set vs a regression cohort
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "the tests".
    ↳ Difference: the set as a whole estimates a rate and may be sampled. The regression cohort is a list of promises, and sampling a promise means sometimes not checking it.
    ↳ Think instead: estimate with the set, block with the cohort.
  • Don't leave the set without an owner or a refresh date.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: once built, it runs by itself and stays green.
    ↳ What goes wrong: traffic shifts, the set still passes, and the green suite now gives assurance about inputs nobody sends.
    ↳ Do instead: name an owner, record the set version on each run, and treat a version unchanged for a year as a warning.
  • Shelf life: cohorts, sourcing and versioning are durable. Synthetic generation of cases keeps improving, and it still needs a real sample to be checked against.

Connections

Path:why eval comes firstgolden datasetsassertionsregression suites and CI
  • Used by LLM as judge: the labelled subset is what a judge is checked against.
  • Owned elsewhere: error bars and paired tests (LLM-Production) covers power and clustering.
  • Owned elsewhere: golden datasets for RAG covers question-and-source pairs.
  • Contrasts with red-teaming: it finds new attacks; this cohort keeps the old ones fixed.
  • Drilled in eval-driven prompt development.

notes.title: Assertion-Based Testing — Check in Code Everything Code Can Check
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: define success criteria and build evaluations · Promptfoo: assertions and metrics · OpenAI: evaluation best practices

TL;DR

An assertion is a rule about the output that code decides: it parses, it cites, every figure is in the source, it is under three sentences. It costs nothing, has no bias and needs no calibration, so it runs first and on every case. Assert the contract, never the wording: an exact-match check on prose that may vary is how a suite turns flaky and gets switched off.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:outputparses to the schema?every figure and cited id found in the inputs?bounds and forbidden stringsexpected tool called?only now a judge, for what code can't decide

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why assertions first? Free, exact, unbiased; they shrink what the judge has to look at.
The highest-value assertion? Every number and date in the answer appears in the source.
How do they go wrong? Exact match on text that may legitimately vary: flaky, then disabled.

The idea

A team wants to catch made-up facts in a billing assistant and starts designing a judge rubric for "hallucination". Weeks in, someone writes twelve lines that pull every number out of the answer and look for it in the retrieved text. It catches more invented figures than the rubric did, on every case, for nothing.

Many properties that sound like judgement have a part that is plain lookup: is the cited id one that was retrieved, is the quoted span in the document, was the escalation tool called. Code decides those exactly.

The line between an assertion and a judge is a test you can apply: given only the output and the inputs, would two reasonable engineers always agree on pass or fail? "Contains a citation": yes. "The tone is appropriate": no. And when the answer is no, the requirement is often unfinished. "Be concise" can't be asserted; "at most three sentences unless the user asked for detail" can.

The trade: assertions verify the contract and say nothing about whether the answer is good. A grounded, valid, short, wrong answer passes all of them.

How it works

The kinds of check, cheapest and most decisive first.

Check Example Catches Flaky?
Parse / schema validates against the declared model broken structure no
Grounding every figure, date and quoted span is in the source; every cited id was retrieved invented facts and citations no
Bounds at most three sentences; under N tokens verbosity drift, truncation rarely
Negative no competitor names; no system-prompt text; no refusal template on an in-scope ask policy and leak failures rarely
Trace escalate_to_human was called behaviour, checked exactly no
Exact text match output equals a stored string almost nothing yes
Rule What actually happens
Filter before judging An output that fails to parse doesn't need its tone judged. Running assertions first is what keeps the judge bill small.
Guarantee beats check Where schema enforcement guarantees the shape, the schema assertion becomes a safety net and the effort moves to grounding.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). Anthropic's guide ranks code-based grading first, "fastest and most reliable"; eval tools ship these checks as built-ins (chapter map, Landscape).
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model fails assertions less often; the assertion is still the only free proof that it didn't. What won't change: a lookup needs no opinion.

Code

Four contract checks on a RAG answer, run on one good and one bad output.

import re
NUM = re.compile(r"\d[\d,]*\.?\d*")
def norm(s): return s.replace(",", "").rstrip(".")

def check(answer: str, source: str, cited: list, retrieved: set) -> list:
    fails = []
    known = {norm(n) for n in NUM.findall(source)}
    invented = [n for n in NUM.findall(answer) if norm(n) not in known]
    if invented:                 fails.append(f"figure not in source: {invented}")
    if not cited:                fails.append("no citation")
    if set(cited) - retrieved:   fails.append(f"cited id not retrieved: {sorted(set(cited) - retrieved)}")
    if len(re.findall(r"[.!?](?:\s|$)", answer)) > 3: fails.append("more than 3 sentences")
    return fails

src = "Invoice 3391: charged 1,200.00 on 4 August. Refund window is 30 days."
print(check("You were charged 1,200.00 on 4 August.", src, ["d7"], {"d7", "d9"}))
print(check("You were charged 1,250.00 and have 45 days.", src, ["d2"], {"d7", "d9"}))
# → []
# → ["figure not in source: ['1,250.00', '45']", "cited id not retrieved: ['d2']"]

Run on Python 3.9, it prints those two lists: the invented amount, the invented window and the citation to a document that was never retrieved.

Measure it

  • Offline: failure rate per assertion on the golden set, new prompt against live. "Better" is fewer contract failures with no rise in any other check.
  • In production: the same assertions on sampled live outputs, counted per rule and per prompt version. A rule that starts failing after a deploy names the regression.
  • Enforced by: the CI gate, where a contract assertion blocks on one failure. At request time the same code is the validator in parsing and repair loops.

Interview

30-second answer: Assertions are deterministic checks on model output: it parses, it cites, every figure appears in the source, it stays under a length. They're free, exact and unbiased, which is why code-based grading comes first and a judge only handles what code can't decide. The discipline is to assert the contract and not the prose, because exact match on text that varies makes a suite flaky and then ignored.

Q · Mechanism — What assertions would you write for a RAG answer endpoint? Structural first: the response parses, required fields are filled, enums are in range. Then grounding, the most valuable and least used: every number and date appears in the retrieved text, every cited id was retrieved, every quoted span is found in a cited chunk. Then negatives: no system-prompt text, no competitor names, length bounds. Then the trace: for an out-of-scope request, the escalation tool was called.

Q · Trade-off — Where is the line between an assertion and a judge? The simpler rung is always the assertion, so I try it first. My test is whether two engineers would always agree on pass or fail from the output and inputs alone. If not, I ask whether the requirement can be sharpened until they would; often it can, and I get a free check plus a clearer prompt. What remains, such as whether the answer addressed the question asked, goes to a judge, and only on outputs that passed the assertions.

Pitfalls

  • "Deterministic checks are too shallow for LLM output"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the output is free text, so the grader should be something that reads.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the commonest and most damaging failures (broken schema, invented citations, figures not in the source) are lookups. A judge spends money to do them worse.
    ↳ Think instead: ask what part of the property is a lookup, and take that part for free.
  • "Catching made-up facts needs an LLM"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: hallucination sounds like a question of meaning.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: for figures, dates, ids and quotations it is a substring search. I spent time on a rubric before trying the search, and the search caught more.
    ↳ Think instead: try the cheap check before deciding a property needs judgement.
  • Not the same: an assertion vs a judge
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both produce pass or fail in the same report.
    ↳ Difference: an assertion's verdict is a fact about the text. A judge's verdict is a model's opinion with its own error rate, which has to be measured.
    ↳ Think instead: gate hard on assertions; treat judge results as measurements with noise.
  • Don't assert on wording that may vary.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a stored ideal answer and an equality check is the fastest test to write.
    ↳ What goes wrong: good answers phrased differently fail, the suite goes red at random, and people stop reading it.
    ↳ Do instead: assert what must hold (a figure, an id, a bound) and leave the phrasing free.
  • Shelf life: the checks are durable. Tool names and built-in assertion lists change yearly.

Connections

Path:golden datasetsassertionsLLM as judgeregression suites and CI
  • Builds on a layered contract: the validator's rules are these tests, run at request time.
  • Contrasts with LLM as judge: a fact about the text against a checked opinion.
  • Owned elsewhere: the RAG triad covers groundedness beyond exact lookup.
  • Enforced by regression suites and CI: the hard gate.
  • Drilled in assertions or an LLM judge.

notes.title: LLM-as-Judge for Prompt Quality — The Judge Is a Prompt, and It Is Tested Before It Tests
notes.html:
References

Zheng et al. 2023: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena · Liu et al. 2023: G-Eval · OpenAI: evaluation best practices · Anthropic: define success criteria and build evaluations

TL;DR

When code can't decide whether an output is good, a second model grades it against a rubric you wrote. That grader is a model with a prompt, so it has every failure the system under test has, plus an error rate that shrinks the differences you are trying to see. Two rules follow: give it yes/no criteria or a pair to compare, never a 1–10 scale; and let it gate nothing until it agrees with human labels on cases it wasn't tuned on.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:write the rubric as yes/no criteriapeople label 100–200 outputstune the rubric on halfmeasure agreement on the other halfpin the judge modeljudge only what passed the assertionsre-measure agreement on a schedule

Recall

Prompt Answer
One output or a pair? A pair when comparing two prompt versions; one output for monitoring, with yes/no criteria.
Why not a 1–10 scale? It needs one consistent ruler across thousands of separate calls; a model doesn't hold one.
What makes a judge usable? Measured agreement with human labels on a held-out set, before any verdict counts.
What does 85% agreement do to a 60/40 result? Shows it as about 57/43: errors pull every difference towards 50/50.
Draw by hand: the rubric Task (compare) · context (question, facts, two replies) · criteria with evidence first · "ignore length" · JSON verdict.

The idea

A team compares two versions of a support prompt with a one-line grader: rate this reply from 1 to 10 for quality. Version B averages slightly higher, and B ships. Later a reviewer reads the scored replies: nearly all of them, including ones the reviewer would call failures, landed in the same narrow band at the top of the scale.

Three things were wrong, none of them the judge model. The grader had no facts to check the reply against, so a confident wrong figure scored well. It was asked for a number on an invented scale, which demands the same internal ruler on every one of thousands of independent calls. And nobody had compared its scores with a person's on even fifty cases.

A judge that works is built like any other production prompt. It gets the ground truth as context. It answers questions with a defined answer: does every figure appear in the account data, yes or no; which of these two replies is better on this criterion. And before its verdicts count, its agreement with human labels is measured on cases the rubric was not adjusted on.

The trade: a judge scales grading to properties code can't check, and in exchange you own a second prompt, a labelled set to keep it honest, and a model call or two per case.

How it works

The rubric is written first, then proved, then allowed to decide.

The dotted edge is the part teams skip: agreement measured once is not a property the judge keeps.

Conceptually, a judge that agrees with the truth with probability a reports this, if its errors don't favour either side:

ŵ       = a·w + (1 − a)·(1 − w)     ← w = true share of cases where B is better
ŵ − ½   = (2a − 1)·(w − ½)          ← every gap from 50/50 shrinks by the factor (2a − 1)
a = 0.85, w = 0.60  →  ŵ = 0.57     ← a 20-point gap is reported as 14
Rule What actually happens
A pair for a comparison "Is A or B better on this criterion?" has a defined answer. Use it when two prompt versions are being compared, in both orders (judge biases).
A checklist for one output With no B, as in production monitoring, ask several yes/no questions and count them. A checklist turns one calibration problem into several discrimination problems.
Give it the facts Without the source or tool result in context, the judge can only grade fluency, and it rewards confident errors.

Evolution

Lineage:2002 BLEU: overlap with a referenceMar 2023 G-Eval: rubric, reasoning first, form-fillingJun 2023 MT-Bench judge study: agreement and four limitations2024–26 provider guides: pairwise or pass/fail, calibrated against human labels
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). Every eval tool ships a judge; how to validate one is still left to the team.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. A stronger judge agrees with people more often. What won't change: it grades against your definition of good, which exists only in your rubric and your labels, and an unmeasured judge is still an unmeasured instrument.
  • Checked on: the agreement figure is for GPT-4 in 2023 (Zheng et al.). OpenAI's guide, as of Oct 2026, recommends "pairwise comparison or pass/fail for more reliability"; Anthropic's recommends a grader that reasons before scoring.

Code

The judge rubric is a prompt, so it is shown as one.

① TASK         Compare two support replies to the same customer question.    ← a comparison, not a score
② CONTEXT      <question>{{q}}</question> <account_data>{{tool_result}}</account_data> ← the facts to check
③ CONTEXT      <reply_a>{{a}}</reply_a> <reply_b>{{b}}</reply_b>               ← untrusted text, as data
④ CONSTRAINTS  For each criterion, quote the text you relied on, then decide.  ← evidence before verdict
⑤ CONSTRAINTS  FACTUAL · COMPLETE · ACTIONABLE: each A, B or tie. Ignore length and tone. ← no scale
⑥ OUTPUT       {"factual": …, "complete": …, "actionable": …, "overall": "A|B|tie"} ← schema-enforced

Against the one-line grader, on the same pair of replies:

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Rate this reply 1–10 for quality: {{reply}} regions ②, ④ and ⑤
On the input a fluent reply quoting a refund amount that is not in the account data a high score loses on FACTUAL, with the mismatched figure quoted
Fails as fluency graded as quality; scores bunched together —
The one edit — ② the ground truth in context: the judge can now check a fact

Break it: a scripted judge with a known error rate, on pairs where B is truly better 60% of the time.

import random
random.seed(3)
def noisy_judge(truth: str, agreement: float) -> str:        # right with probability `agreement`
    return truth if random.random() < agreement else ("A" if truth == "B" else "B")

pairs = ["B"] * 6000 + ["A"] * 4000                          # B is truly better on 60% of cases
for a in (1.0, 0.85, 0.70):
    wins = sum(noisy_judge(t, a) == "B" for t in pairs) / len(pairs)
    print(a, round(wins, 3))
# look for: the observed win rate of B as the judge's agreement falls
# naive belief predicts: 0.60 every time, because errors "average out"

Run on Python 3.9, it prints 0.6, 0.563 and 0.541. More cases don't move them back towards 0.60.

Measure it

  • Offline: agreement with human labels on a held-out labelled set (100–200 cases to start), against the previous rubric. Read the disagreements by category: a cluster in one topic is a rubric defect, not noise.
  • In production: agreement re-measured on freshly labelled samples; judge cost as a share of inference spend; judge scores next to a fixed golden set, so a drifting score can be told from drifting traffic.
  • Enforced by: the rule that a rubric can't gate until its measured agreement is on record with the judge model version. The judge's verdict itself is a model's opinion.

Interview

30-second answer: When output quality isn't checkable in code, a second model grades it. I use a pair when comparing two prompt versions and a yes/no checklist when grading one output, never a 1-to-10 scale. Zheng and colleagues found GPT-4 agreeing with people over eighty percent of the time, about what people manage with each other. But the judge is itself a prompt, so I measure its agreement with human labels on held-out cases before any number it emits counts.

Q · Mechanism — One output or a pair: how do you choose? A pair when there are two versions to compare, which is most prompt work. "Which is better on this criterion?" is a discrimination with a defined answer. A score for one output needs a consistent internal ruler across independent calls, and in practice the scores bunch together and hide the differences I care about. With no second version, as in monitoring, I still avoid the scale: several yes/no criteria, counted.

Q · Trade-off — Your judge agrees with people 85% of the time. Is that enough to gate a release? It depends on the size of the difference I'm gating on. The simpler rung is an assertion, and anything code can check shouldn't reach the judge. For what remains, 85% is plenty to catch a large regression. For a three-point improvement it isn't: the judge's error is several times the effect, and it shrinks the observed gap as well. So I read the disagreements. Scattered ones I can live with; a cluster in the area I'm changing disqualifies the judge there.

Q · Failure — Judge scores rise for three months with no prompt change. What happened? Three candidates. The judge model changed under an alias, so the trend crosses two instruments: I check the model version on each run. Traffic got easier: I compare with the fixed golden set, which doesn't drift. Or someone has been tuning prompts against the judge, and outputs have moved towards what it rewards: I re-measure agreement on fresh human labels.

Q · Design — Forty teams ship prompts and need quality gates. Design the evaluation layer. The binding constraint is that an unvalidated judge is worse than no gate, because its numbers look like evidence. So teams own rubrics and the platform owns validation: a team registers a rubric with a labelled set, the platform measures held-out agreement, and the rubric may gate only above a bar. Underneath, assertions run on every case; the judge sees what passed, in both orders, with its model pinned; people review the pairs it contradicted itself on. I'd watch agreement decay first, then judge cost. It sits in the evaluation plane of the prompt-layer reference architecture.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Judge agreement with people over 80% GPT-4 as judge, MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, 2023; "the same level of agreement between humans" cited (Zheng et al. 2023)
Correlation with human ratings Spearman 0.514 G-Eval with GPT-4, summarisation, 2023 cited (Liu et al. 2023)
Shrink factor at 85% agreement 0.70 2 × 0.85 − 1; a 60/40 result reads 57/43 derived

Pitfalls

  • "A frontier model is smart enough to judge, so the rubric needs little work"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the model writes good critiques when you chat with it.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: capability is not calibration. With a vague rubric and no facts, a strong model grades fluency and length. With criteria, context and evidence first, the same model gives usable verdicts.
    ↳ Think instead: the rubric is the instrument; the model only runs it.
  • "Over 80% agreement means the judge is right 80% of the time"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: agreement reads like accuracy.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it matches a human label, and people disagree with each other at about the same rate. And the error is not harmless noise: it pulls every measured difference towards 50/50 (Break it).
    ↳ Think instead: agreement tells you how much smaller your effects will look.
  • "A 1–10 score is fine if the rubric wording is consistent"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a number per output is easy to average and chart.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: consistent wording doesn't create a consistent ruler. My scores sat in a narrow band across good and bad outputs, so the metric couldn't separate them. Switching to pairs and yes/no checks brought the separation back.
    ↳ Think instead: change the question's shape before polishing its wording.
  • Not the same: agreement on the tuning cases vs on held-out cases
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "agreement with human labels".
    ↳ Difference: the first was reached by adjusting the rubric until it matched those labels. Only the second predicts how the judge behaves on new outputs.
    ↳ Think instead: split the labelled set before touching the rubric, and quote the held-out figure.
  • Don't tune prompts against a judge without going back to people.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the judge is fast, so it becomes the target of every iteration and of any optimiser.
    ↳ What goes wrong: outputs drift towards whatever the judge rewards. Its scores rise honestly while human-perceived quality doesn't.
    ↳ Do instead: re-measure agreement on fresh labels on a schedule, and whenever scores climb without an explanation.
  • Shelf life: agreement figures belong to one judge model, one benchmark and one year; re-measure on your own rubric. The need to validate the grader does not expire.

Connections

Path:assertionsLLM as judgejudge biasesregression suites and CI
  • Builds on anatomy of a production prompt: a rubric uses the same regions.
  • Owned elsewhere: LLM-as-a-judge and human eval (LLM-Production) cover judge mechanics and labelling.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the calibration cohort is the judge's own test set.
  • Attacked by indirect prompt injection: the replies being judged are untrusted text in the judge's window.
  • Used by DSPy: a judge is often the metric an optimiser climbs.
  • Drilled in assertions or an LLM judge.

notes.title: Judge Biases — Position, Verbosity, Self-Preference, and the Swap That Exposes Them
notes.html:
References

Wang et al. 2023: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators · Zheng et al. 2023: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena · Liu et al. 2023: G-Eval · OpenAI: evaluation best practices

TL;DR

A judge's errors are not random. It leans towards a position, towards the longer answer, towards text from its own model family, and it can't grade what it couldn't solve. A bias has a direction, so more cases make the wrong answer more precise, not less wrong. The counter is a protocol, not a sentence in the rubric: run every pair in both orders, and when the two verdicts disagree, record "no measurement", not a tie.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:pair (A, B)judge with A firstjudge with B firstun-swap the second verdictcount it
flag: no measurementsample the flagged pairs for a persontrack the flip rate

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four named limitations? Position, verbosity, self-enhancement, limited reasoning (Zheng et al. 2023).
How large can position bias be? Order alone made Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries (Wang et al. 2023).
What do you do when the two orders disagree? Flag the pair as unmeasured; don't average it into a tie.
What is the flip rate? The share of pairs whose verdict changes when the order is swapped.
Draw by hand: the swap App sends (A, B), then (B, A); un-swap; agree → count, disagree → flag → person.

The idea

You compare the live prompt (A) with a candidate (B) using a pairwise judge. A is always shown first. A wins comfortably, and the candidate is dropped. Then someone reruns the comparison with B first, and B wins.

Nothing about the replies changed. Wang and colleagues showed the size this effect can reach: with ChatGPT as the evaluator, changing only the order of the two responses let Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries.

That is one of four limitations Zheng and colleagues named, tabled below.

What makes these dangerous is that each has a direction. Random error averages out over a thousand cases. A lean towards the longer answer is present in all thousand, so the suite reports a precise number that is wrong the same way every time.

So the fix is done outside the judge: both orders, a judge from another family, a reference answer where one exists. A rubric line saying "ignore length" is worth adding, and it is a request.

The trade: the swap doubles the judge calls, and what it buys is knowing which verdicts were decided by content and which by position.

How it works

Each limitation, how you'd see it in your own data, and what you change.

Bias What the judge does How you detect it What you change
Position prefers a slot, whatever is in it flip rate under an order swap both orders; a disagreement is flagged
Verbosity prefers the longer reply among decided pairs, how often the longer side wins, against the same share in human labels separate criteria, so no single "quality" axis stands in for length; a request to ignore length
Self-enhancement prefers output from its own model family re-judge a sample with a judge from another family and compare a judge from a different provider than the system under test
Limited reasoning marks a wrong solution right when it can't solve the problem accuracy on problems with known answers a reference answer in the rubric, or an executable check instead of a judge

The swap, as it runs for one pair.

The flagged pairs are where the judge is least sure: the best use of a person's time.

Rule What actually happens
A flag is not a tie "Equally good" and "the judge couldn't tell" are different findings. Averaging the two orders into 50/50 makes them look the same in your data.
Keep a standing panel A fixed set of pairs with human verdicts, re-run on a schedule, giving three numbers: agreement, flip rate, and how often the longer side wins.

Evolution

Lineage:Mar 2023 G-Eval notes that LLM evaluators may favour LLM-written textMay 2023 Wang et al. measure position bias and propose three calibrationsJun 2023 Zheng et al. name position, verbosity, self-enhancement and limited reasoning2024–26 provider guides name position and verbosity bias
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). The biases are documented and named in OpenAI's guide; a standard protocol in tools is not yet universal.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. A stronger judge solves more of what it grades. What won't change: a judge from the same family as the system it grades has a reason to prefer it, and only running both orders shows whether position decided a verdict.
  • Checked on: the 66-of-80 result used ChatGPT as evaluator in 2023; the size on a current judge with your rubric is unknown until you measure your flip rate.

Code

The protocol: both orders, the reversed verdict un-swapped, a disagreement flagged.

UNSWAP = {"A": "B", "B": "A", "tie": "tie"}

def judge_pair(judge, rubric, a: str, b: str) -> dict:
    fwd = judge(rubric, first=a, second=b)             # verdict names a slot: "A", "B" or "tie"
    rev = UNSWAP[judge(rubric, first=b, second=a)]     # same pair, other order, then un-swapped
    if fwd != rev:                                     # position, not content, decided at least one
        return {"winner": None, "flagged": True}       # no measurement: do not score it 50/50
    return {"winner": fwd, "flagged": False}

Break it: a scripted judge that picks the first slot unless it is clearly worse, on 100 pairs where B is truly better on 80.

def biased_judge(first: float, second: float) -> str:        # scripted: quality in, slot out
    return "first" if first >= second - 0.15 else "second"   # picks slot 1 unless clearly worse

def swapped(a: float, b: float) -> str:
    fwd = "A" if biased_judge(a, b) == "first" else "B"      # A shown first
    rev = "B" if biased_judge(b, a) == "first" else "A"      # B shown first
    return fwd if fwd == rev else "flag"                     # disagreement = no measurement

pairs = [(0.5, 0.6)] * 60 + [(0.5, 0.9)] * 20 + [(0.8, 0.4)] * 20    # (quality of A, of B)
one_order = [("A" if biased_judge(a, b) == "first" else "B") for a, b in pairs]
both = [swapped(a, b) for a, b in pairs]
print("A first only:", one_order.count("A"), one_order.count("B"))
print("both orders :", both.count("A"), both.count("B"), both.count("flag"))
# look for: who wins with A always shown first, against the count after the swap
# naive belief predicts: the same winner either way, because B is better on 80 of 100 pairs

Run on Python 3.9, it prints A first only: 80 20 and both orders : 20 20 60. In one order the worse prompt wins 80 to 20. After the swap the honest reading is 20 each and 60 undecided: the swap doesn't recover B's narrow wins, it stops you reporting them for A.

Measure it

  • Offline: on the standing panel, flip rate and the longer-side win share against the previous rubric and judge version. "Better" is a lower flip rate with agreement not falling.
  • In production: the flip rate per eval run. A jump with no rubric change means the judge model changed, or the two candidates have become too alike for this rubric to separate.
  • Enforced by: the eval harness, which runs both orders and refuses to count a flagged pair. "Ignore length and position" in the rubric is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: LLM judges have documented, directional biases. Position: in one 2023 study, changing only the order let a weaker model beat a stronger one on 66 of 80 queries. Verbosity: longer answers score higher. Self-enhancement: a judge favours its own family. The counters are protocol: run both orders and flag disagreements, split the rubric into criteria so length can't stand in for quality, and use a judge from a different family.

Q · Mechanism — Walk through each bias and what you do about it. Position: both orders, and a disagreement is recorded as unmeasured and sampled for a person. Verbosity: separate criteria and a request to ignore length, then a check of how often the longer side wins compared with human labels. Self-enhancement: a judge from another provider than the model being graded. Limited reasoning: no judge at all where a reference answer or an executable check exists.

Q · Trade-off — The swap doubles judge cost. Is it worth it? The simpler rung is one order, and I'd keep it if my measured flip rate is near zero. So I measure first: a few hundred pairs in both orders. With a flip rate in the tens of percent, a single-order verdict isn't a cheap measurement, it's no measurement, and the money is already wasted.

Q · Failure — The flip rate was 8% for months and jumped to 30% overnight. Why? Two suspects. First: the judge model changed under an alias. I check the model version stored with each run. Second: the candidates converged. A judge flips constantly on two near-identical outputs, so the jump can mean the rubric has reached the limit of what it can separate. The flip rate moves before agreement does, so I alert on it.

Q · Design — Design a debiasing protocol for CI with a cost budget. Full rigour on every case is unaffordable, so I tier by the decision. Assertions absorb everything checkable; they have none of these biases. Per pull request: a judge on a sample by cohort, one order, with a rubric whose flip rate is already known to be low, used only for large regressions. Per release candidate: the full set, both orders, flagged pairs excluded from the estimate and sampled for people. Alongside, the standing panel runs weekly with the pinned judge version. I'd watch the longer-side share first, since no default dashboard shows it. The gate itself is in regression suites and CI.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Position bias, worst case shown 66 of 80 queries Vicuna-13B "beating" ChatGPT by order alone, ChatGPT as evaluator, 2023 cited (Wang et al. 2023)
Single order against both orders 80–20 for A, then 20–20 with 60 flagged the scripted judge above, 100 pairs measured (Python 3.9, 12 Oct 2026)

Pitfalls

  • "Judge bias is noise, and noise averages out over a large suite"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: that is how sampling error behaves, and a big suite feels safe.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a bias points one way in every case. A thousand cases judged by something that prefers length give a tight interval around the wrong answer.
    ↳ Think instead: more cases shrink variance; only a changed protocol removes bias.
  • "Use the strongest model as judge and the biases go away"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: strength helps with most things, and limited reasoning really does improve.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the biases were documented on the strongest judges of their year. And the strongest model is often the one you are evaluating, which is the self-enhancement setup.
    ↳ Think instead: choose the judge for independence from the system under test, then for strength.
  • "We validated the judge against human labels, so it is unbiased"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: agreement was the one check everyone told me to run, and it passed.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: agreement and bias are different properties. My labellers had been asked for an overall preference and were rewarding length as well; the judge agreed with them and flipped on order.
    ↳ Think instead: label against separate criteria, and measure the flip rate as well as agreement.
  • Not the same: a tie vs "the judge couldn't tell"
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: averaging the two orders gives 50/50 for both.
    ↳ Difference: a tie is a finding about the outputs: they are equally good. A disagreement across orders is a finding about the judge: it has no stable verdict here.
    ↳ Think instead: keep a separate flagged count; only it tells you where to look.
  • Don't use the protocol as a substitute for a better rubric.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the swap is mechanical and the rubric is hard thinking.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a vague "which is better?" in both orders gives you a carefully measured, mostly flagged result, as in Break it.
    ↳ Do instead: when the flip rate is high, sharpen the criteria first; the swap then confirms the improvement.
  • Shelf life: the magnitudes are from 2023 models and will differ on yours. That a bias has a direction, and that only a swap reveals position effects, will not change.

Connections

Path:LLM as judgejudge biasesregression suites and CIA/B tests
  • Builds on prompt sensitivity: position bias is order sensitivity, in the judge's own prompt.
  • Owned elsewhere: LLM-as-a-judge (LLM-Production) covers how judges are built and calibrated.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the standing panel is a calibration cohort.
  • Used by auto-optimisation: an optimiser climbing a biased judge amplifies the bias.
  • Costed in cost modelling: judge calls are inference spend.
  • Drilled in assertions or an LLM judge.

notes.title: Regression Suites & CI for Prompts — Contracts Block Exactly, Measurements Block Outside the Noise
notes.html:
References

OpenAI: evaluation best practices · Anthropic: a statistical approach to model evaluations · Anthropic: define success criteria and build evaluations · Promptfoo: assertions and metrics

TL;DR

Prompt CI is code CI with two assumptions removed: the tests are noisy, and an edit to one clause can move any case. So the gate has two parts that must not be mixed. Contracts (schema, safety, one case per past incident) block on a single failure. Measurements (a judged pass rate) block only when the drop is larger than the noise. And the average is not enough: keep each case's history, and compare with a frozen baseline as well as with the last version.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:change to the tupleassertions on every caseblock, name the case
judge a sample + contract cohorts in full, paired with the live versionblock, show worst casesrecord the runpasscompare with the frozen baseline

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why can't you run only the tests near the change? Prompt effects are non-local: any clause can move any case.
The two kinds of gate? Contracts block on one failure; measurements block outside measured noise.
What is recorded with every run? Prompt version, model version, settings, tool definitions, golden-set version, judge version, scores.
What does the average hide? Four cases fixed and four broken reads as no change.
Draw by hand: the gate Assertions on all → contract broken? → block. Else paired judge → beyond noise? → block. Else record, pass, check drift.
What catches slow erosion? A frozen baseline: each change passes its own gate while the total falls.

The idea

A team's prompt suite fails at random now and then. People re-run it until it is green, and someone loosens the threshold so it stops blocking. A month later the suite is still green on the day a change ships that makes the assistant promise refunds it can't give.

Three different things had been merged into one number. A few exact-match checks on wording that may vary: those were bugs in the tests. A judged quality score that moves a little between identical runs: that is noise, and it needs a threshold derived from measurement. And a handful of cases that must never fail, such as the refund rule: those need no threshold at all. Loosening everything together turned all three into a gate that blocks nothing.

Two properties make prompt CI unlike code CI. A test's result is a sample, so pass and fail need a margin. And a prompt has no call graph: rewording the tone instruction can change whether a tool is called, so "run only what the change touches" is unsound.

The trade: a gate that is honest about noise blocks less often than people expect, and that is the price of a gate nobody learns to bypass.

How it works

One gate, two rules, one record.

A block always names cases. A blocked change with no example to look at gets overridden.

The decision rule: which change runs which suite.

What changed What runs Why
Any prompt text (an instruction, an example, the order of regions) assertions on every case; contract cohorts in full; judge on a sample by cohort effects are non-local, so no subset by "area"
The output contract the above, plus the consumer's own parsing tests the reader of the output changed too
Model version or sampling settings the full set, judge in both orders a new model is a new tuple: model-upgrade migration
The judge rubric or judge model the judge's own panel, not the product suite the instrument changed, not the product
Nothing (nightly) the full set on the live tuple provider-side drift that no commit caused
Rule What actually happens
Pair the comparison Both versions run on the same cases, and the gate tests the per-case differences. Shared difficulty cancels, so the noise to clear is smaller.
Measure the noise Re-run the unchanged live prompt a few times; the spread sets the threshold. A guessed threshold is either flaky or toothless, and you can't tell which.
Keep per-case history Alert on any case that went from pass to fail, whatever the average did.
Hold a frozen baseline Compare each release with a fixed old version too. Twelve changes that each lose 1.5 points under a 2-point gate lose 18.

Evolution

Lineage:2022–23 prompts changed in a playground and pasted into code2023–24 assertion files run in CI by open-source toolsNov 2024 error bars and paired differences argued for evals2025–26 provider guides: "run evals on every change"
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). Running a suite in CI is common; separating contracts from measurements and gating on measured noise is not yet.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model regresses less per change and still regresses, and each new model is itself a change to gate. What won't change: a noisy test needs a margin, and a promise needs none.

Code

The gate: ① contracts, ② a paired comparison, ③ a noise threshold, ④ the cases that flipped.

import math
def gate(base: dict, new: dict, contracts: set) -> str:
    broken = sorted(c for c in contracts if base[c] and not new[c])
    if broken:                                         # ① contract: one failure blocks, no statistics
        return f"BLOCK contract {broken}"
    d = [new[c] - base[c] for c in base]               # ② paired: the same cases on both sides
    mean = sum(d) / len(d)
    se = math.sqrt(sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in d) / (len(d) - 1) / len(d))
    flips = sorted(c for c in base if base[c] and not new[c])
    if mean < -1.96 * se:                              # ③ measurement: block only outside the noise
        return f"BLOCK regression {mean:+.3f}, look at {flips[:5]}"
    return f"PASS {mean:+.3f} ± {1.96 * se:.3f}, newly failing: {flips}"   # ④ per-case history

Break it: an edit that fixes four cases and breaks four others, one of them guarding a past incident.

base = {f"t{i:02d}": int(i < 40) for i in range(50)}   # 40 of 50 cases pass on the live prompt
new = dict(base)
for c in ("t40", "t41", "t42", "t43"): new[c] = 1      # the edit fixes four cases
for c in ("t03", "t04", "t05", "t06"): new[c] = 0      # and breaks four others
print(sum(base.values()) / 50, sum(new.values()) / 50)
print(gate(base, new, contracts=set()))
print(gate(base, new, contracts={"t05"}))              # t05 guards a past incident
# look for: the aggregate before and after, against what the gate reports
# naive belief predicts: an unchanged pass rate means nothing regressed

Run on Python 3.9, it prints 0.8 0.8, then PASS +0.000 ± 0.112, newly failing: ['t03', 't04', 't05', 't06'], then BLOCK contract ['t05']. The pass rate didn't move. Only the per-case list shows that four behaviours stopped working, and only the contract cohort stops the release.

Measure it

  • Offline: the paired difference against the live version on the same set version, with its interval, plus the list of newly failing cases. "Better" is no contract failure and a difference not below the noise band.
  • In production: per suite, the flake rate and the bypass rate. A gate overridden twice a week has stopped being a control. Then the drift line against the frozen baseline.
  • Enforced by: the CI gate on the merge or release path, with the override logged and named. A suite that runs but can't block is a report.

Interview

30-second answer: Prompt CI is code CI with two differences. The tests are stochastic, so the threshold has to account for run-to-run noise or the suite goes flaky and gets disabled. And effects are non-local, so I can't run a subset based on what changed. I split the gate: contracts like schema, safety and past incidents block on one failure, and judged quality blocks only on a paired drop beyond measured noise. I keep per-case history, because the average hides swaps.

Q · Mechanism — What is in a prompt regression suite? Four cohorts from the golden set: typical, edge, adversarial, and one regression case per incident. Each case carries its assertions, an optional rubric, and a tag for the behaviour it protects, so a failure reads "the refusal cohort regressed". And every run carries the tuple, or its score can't be interpreted a month later.

Q · Trade-off — Three percent of cases fail at random. Fix the cases or loosen the gate? Neither as stated. The simpler rung is to delete the exact-match checks on free text; those are test bugs and usually a good share of the flakiness. What remains is real sampling noise, and for that I gate on the paired aggregate with a threshold from re-running an unchanged prompt. The contract cases get no tolerance at all. Loosening uniformly is the one option that makes all three worse.

Q · Failure — Every change passed the gate, yet quality is clearly worse after six months. How? Three mechanisms. Erosion under the threshold: each change lost a little and nothing tracked the total, so I add a frozen baseline with its own alert. Masking: changes fixed some cases and broke others at a flat average; per-case history shows it. Staleness: the set was sampled long ago and now passes on inputs nobody sends, so I check the set version's age and how many recent complaints resemble a case in it.

Q · Design — Design prompt CI for forty teams on shared infrastructure with a cost budget. The binding constraint is cost and duration: a suite too slow to wait for gets routed around. So tiers are set by the platform. Per commit: assertions on every case, seconds, free. Per pull request: contract cohorts in full plus a judged sample. Per release candidate: the full set, both judge orders, the paired gate. Nightly: the full set on the live tuple. Shared services: a results store keyed by the tuple, a verdict cache by content hash, a job that re-measures each suite's noise, and golden sets as versioned artifacts with owners. I'd watch the bypass rate first. It is the evaluation plane of the prompt-layer reference architecture.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Erosion under a 2-point gate 18 points 12 changes × 1.5 points each, every one passing derived
Masked regression pass rate 0.80 → 0.80 with 4 cases newly failing the experiment above, 50 cases measured (Python 3.9, 12 Oct 2026)

Pitfalls

  • "Prompt CI is unit testing with a different assertion library"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the tooling looks the same: a file of cases, a runner, a green tick.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a unit test is deterministic and scoped to the code it calls. A prompt test is a sample, and any clause can affect it.
    ↳ Think instead: a margin for noise, and no test selection by area.
  • "The aggregate didn't drop, so nothing regressed"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one number on a dashboard is what people look at.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the average is a sum. An edit that fixes four cases and breaks four reads as no change (Break it), and months of that swap which behaviours work under a flat line.
    ↳ Think instead: the unit of regression is the case, not the score.
  • "The suite is flaky, so loosen the thresholds until it stops blocking"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it removes the daily irritation in one edit.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: I had merged test bugs, real noise and hard promises into one gate. Loosening all three left a suite that was green in the week a regression reached customers.
    ↳ Think instead: fix the bad tests, measure the noise, and give promises no tolerance.
  • Not the same: a contract vs a measurement
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are rows in the same report with a pass rate.
    ↳ Difference: a contract is a promise checked by code on named cases, where one failure is a defect. A measurement is an estimate of a rate, where one failure is expected.
    ↳ Think instead: ask of each check, "would one failure block a release?", and file it accordingly.
  • Don't build four tiers for one prompt and thirty cases.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the tiered design is the one in every architecture talk.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the machinery costs more to keep than the suite it schedules.
    ↳ Do instead: run everything on every change until the run takes longer than people will wait; then tier.
  • Shelf life: the two kinds of gate, pairing and per-case history are durable. Runner tools change quickly; one hosted eval platform is being shut down this year (chapter map, Landscape).

Connections

Path:assertionsjudge biasesregression suites and CIeval-driven developmentdecoupled release
  • Builds on the prompt as a coupled system: the gate runs on a change to any part of the tuple.
  • Owned elsewhere: evals in CI and error bars and paired tests (LLM-Production) own the statistics.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the cohorts are what the gate runs.
  • Shipped by prompt versioning: the run record points at a version; a pass promotes it.
  • Used by model-upgrade migration: the suite is the triage tool for a new model.
  • Drilled in a model upgrade regressed the prompts.

notes.title: A/B Testing Prompts in Production — What Users Did, Against What the Suite Scored
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: a statistical approach to model evaluations · OpenAI: evaluation best practices · Anthropic: prompt caching

TL;DR

The offline suite says B scores better on your definition of correct. An A/B test says whether users behaved differently. Randomise by user or session, never by request, and count users, not requests, as your sample. Its second job matters as much as the first: when online and offline disagree, the defect is usually in the golden set.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:B passes the offline gatefix the metric, guardrails and end date in advanceassign each user to A or B by a stable hashrun to the end dateanalyse per usership, drop, or report "no difference"fix the golden set

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is the randomisation unit? The user or session; one person must not see both prompts.
Why isn't request count the sample size? A user's requests are correlated; ten from one person are not ten observations.
What does it cost beyond time? Real users get the worse variant, and two variants mean two cache prefixes.

The idea

A candidate prompt wins offline by four points on a judged metric. It ships to everyone. Escalations to human agents go up.

Both results are true. The suite scored single replies against a definition of correct the team wrote. Users reacted to something the suite has no case for: the new prompt asks a clarifying question where the old one answered, and over a conversation that reads as stalling.

An online test measures behaviour that only real use produces. The reliable signals are the negative ones: an escalation, a thumbs-down, the same question rephrased, a session abandoned. Positive feedback is rare and comes from the already pleased.

It is slow and it is paid for in user experience, so it follows the offline gate and never replaces it.

The trade: an A/B test answers the question that matters, a few times a quarter, at the cost of exposing users to the variant that loses.

How it works

What each instrument can tell you.

Offline suite Online A/B test
Answers does it score better on my cases? did users behave better?
Time to a result minutes days to weeks
Ground truth your checks and labels behaviour
Iterations many per day a few per quarter
Blind to conversation-level and experience effects anything users don't react to
Role the gate, first confirmation, and an audit of the gate

Conceptually, correlated requests shrink the sample. With m requests per user and correlation ρ between a user's requests:

design effect   = 1 + (m − 1)·ρ          ← how much the variance is inflated
effective n     = requests / design effect
m = 10, ρ = 0.2 → 2.8                    ← 100,000 requests carry about 35,700 requests' worth
Rule What actually happens
Decide before you look One decision metric, the guardrails that may only fail (cost per request, latency, error rate, safety-filter rate) and the end date are written down first.
Don't peek and stop Checking daily and stopping at the first significant reading inflates false wins. Fix the horizon, or use a method built for sequential looks.
Skip it when nothing a user sees can change A schema fix or a cache-friendly reorder with identical outputs is fully covered offline.
Insist on it for conversational behaviour Refusals, tone, and how much the assistant asks before acting are what single-reply cases under-measure.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). Controlled experiments are decades old in web products; applying them to prompt variants adds the cache-prefix cost and the judged-metric audit.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A stronger model changes which variant wins. What won't change: only users reveal whether your definition of correct matches what they need.

Code

The experiment as a record, written before any traffic is split.

experiment: billing-assistant-v42-vs-v41
unit: user_id                      # stable hash of the user, not the request
split: {A: 0.5, B: 0.5}
decision_metric: escalation_rate   # lower is better; per user
guardrails:                        # can only fail the variant, never win it
  cost_per_request: "+10% max"
  p95_latency_ms: "+15% max"
  safety_filter_rate: "no increase"
minimum_detectable_change: 1.0 point
ends: 2026-10-30                   # fixed in advance; no early stop on a good day
analysis: per-user rates, standard errors clustered on user_id

Measure it

  • Offline: before the test, the two variants on the golden set; afterwards, whether the offline winner and the online winner agree. Track that agreement over experiments: it is the quality score of your suite.
  • In production: the decision metric per user by variant, guardrails by variant, and cache-read share by variant, since each prefix is cached separately.
  • Enforced by: the rollout system, which assigns by a stable hash and holds the split to the end date; and a pre-registered record like the one above, reviewed before launch.

Interview

30-second answer: Online A/B checks whether the offline metric tracks user value. I split by user or session, never by request, and measure behaviour: escalations, thumbs-down, rephrased questions, task completion. The statistics are where it goes wrong: a user's requests are correlated, so the sample is users, and naive request-level errors make an underpowered test look decisive. I fix the metric, guardrails and end date before launch.

Q · Mechanism — What do you measure, given quality isn't observable in production? Behaviour that shows whether the answer worked. Negative events first, because they are unambiguous and cheap to log: escalation, thumbs-down, a rephrase in the same session, abandonment. Then task outcomes where the product has them; those are delayed, so they decide and the faster ones monitor.

Q · Trade-off — Offline says B wins by four points. Do you still need the A/B test? The simpler rung is to ship on the offline gate, and I do for changes that can't alter what a user sees. For anything touching refusals, tone, or asking against assuming, I run it, because single-reply cases under-measure those. A small judged gain is also where the offline number is least reliable. And a disagreement between the two is worth the test by itself: it tells me what the golden set is missing.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Design effect 2.8 10 requests per user, assumed correlation 0.2: 1 + 9 × 0.2 derived
Effective sample about 35,700 100,000 requests ÷ 2.8 derived

Pitfalls

  • "Real users are the ground truth, so A/B testing replaces offline evals"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: behaviour is the thing you finally care about.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: online is slow and paid for by users who get the losing variant. A team with only online tests iterates a few times a quarter and hears about regressions from customers.
    ↳ Think instead: offline removes the losers cheaply; online confirms the survivor.
  • "We have plenty of traffic, so any experiment is well powered"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the request counter is the biggest number on the dashboard.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the unit is the user. With many requests per user my effective sample was a fraction of the request count, and wins shipped on the naive analysis didn't hold up when repeated.
    ↳ Think instead: count randomised units, and cluster the errors on them.
  • Not the same: an A/B test vs a canary
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both send a share of traffic to a new version.
    ↳ Difference: a canary is a safety check: small share, short, watching for breakage, rolled back on an alarm. An A/B test is a measurement: balanced, run to a fixed date, read for a difference.
    ↳ Think instead: canary to find out whether it is broken; A/B to find out whether it is better.
  • Don't run many prompt experiments at once.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: traffic looks plentiful and every team has a variant.
    ↳ What goes wrong: variants interact, each arm gets fewer users, and each live variant is another cache prefix, so every arm costs more (provider prompt caching).
    ↳ Do instead: queue them; give the offline suite the job of choosing which few deserve traffic.
  • Shelf life: the method is durable. Cache pricing, which sets the cost of a second variant, is volatile.

Connections

Path:regression suites and CIA/B testsdecoupled releaseobservability
  • Builds on golden datasets: a disagreement with offline becomes new cases.
  • Owned elsewhere: production eval and error bars and paired tests (LLM-Production) cover online metrics and clustering.
  • Owned elsewhere: A/B testing RAG changes covers retrieval-side variants.
  • Costed in context ordering for cache hit rate: two variants split the cached prefix.
  • Drilled in offline suite or A/B test.

notes.title: Measuring Prompt Sensitivity — The Noise Floor Under Every Comparison
notes.html:
References

Sclar et al. 2023: sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design (FormatSpread) · Anthropic: a statistical approach to model evaluations

TL;DR

Change something that shouldn't matter (a separator, the order of examples, the wording of the user's input) and score the same golden set each time. The spread of those scores is your noise floor: a gain smaller than it is not a gain. Why prompts behave this way is in prompt sensitivity.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change

Recall

Prompt Answer
Perturbation test Vary form only (separators, casing, example order) and report the score range.
Two uses of the spread The smallest gain worth believing; and a wide spread is itself a defect.

The idea

A new prompt beats the old one by two points: the instruction you rewrote, or the colon you replaced with a dash? Run both prompts in several equivalent formats: if each one's own scores range over six points, two points decides nothing.

What you vary Tells you
Format (separators, spacing, casing) the noise floor for any comparison
Input paraphrase whether users phrasing things differently get different answers

Report a range, not a point, and compare ranges. Each variant costs one more run of the suite.

Evolution

Lineage:2021 example order shown to swing few-shot accuracyOct 2023 FormatSpread: up to 76 accuracy points apart for LLaMA-2-13B in few-shot classification. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026).

Code
