def spread(score, variants: list) -> tuple:
    s = [score(v) for v in variants]
    return min(s), max(s), round(max(s) - min(s), 3)
variants = ["Q: {q}\nA:", "Question: {q}\nAnswer:", "QUESTION - {q}\nANSWER -", "{q}\n\n"]
canned = dict(zip(variants, [0.81, 0.84, 0.78, 0.80]))   # stand-ins
print(spread(canned.get, variants))                                # → (0.78, 0.84, 0.06)

notes.title: Component vs End-to-End Eval — Gate on the Whole, Diagnose by the Part
notes.html:
References

Opsahl-Ong et al. 2024: Optimizing Instructions and Demonstrations for Multi-Stage Language Model Programs · Khattab et al. 2023: DSPy · OpenAI: evaluation best practices

TL;DR

In a chain of prompts, an end-to-end score tells you the system got worse and not where. A per-stage score tells you one stage got better and not whether that helped. Record each stage's result and the final outcome on the same run; then ask which stage's failure predicts a failed run.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:one traced rungrade each stage's outputgrade the final answerstore all of it under one run idper stage: failure rate when it was wrong minus when it was rightfix the stage with the largest gapgate on end to end

Recall

Prompt Answer
What can't end-to-end tell you? Which stage caused the failure.
What can't a stage score tell you? Whether the local gain survives the stages after it.
What joins them? Per-stage results and the final outcome recorded on the same runs.

The idea

A three-prompt chain rewrites the user's question, retrieves, then answers. The team improves the rewriter: on its own test, "is this a well-formed standalone question?", it now scores higher. End-to-end accuracy drops.

The rewriter now produces tidy, formal questions. The documents are written the way customers talk, and the retriever matched the messy original better.

A stage's best behaviour depends on its neighbours. Its real input is whatever the previous stage emits (headers, half sentences, duplicates), not the clean text you'd write by hand. So a stage tested alone, on hand-written inputs, is tested against a contract the chain never honours.

End-to-end is the gate, because it is what users get. Stage scores are diagnostic, and they become useful only when joined to the outcome of the same run.

The trade: recording every stage on every run costs storage and a grader per stage, and turns "which stage?" from days of guessing into a query.

How it works

The three views, and what each is for.

Stage score End-to-end score Joined on the same runs
Answers is this stage right? does the system work? which stage's failure sinks a run?
Finds the cause within one stage no yes
Valid as a gate no yes yes

For stage s, the number to look at is a difference of two failure rates:

attribution(s) = P(run fails | s wrong) − P(run fails | s right)

A large gap marks a bottleneck. A gap near zero means the chain already absorbs that stage's mistakes.

Rule What actually happens
Harvest stage labels from traces Grade what the stage really received and produced. Hand-written stage inputs test a format that never occurs.
Localise a regression by substitution Run the new chain, and for one stage swap in the old version's output for the same case. If the result recovers, that stage is responsible.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). Tracing per call is common; per-stage grading joined to outcomes is done by teams with multi-stage pipelines and optimisers.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. A stronger model makes each stage fail less, and some chains collapse into one call (prompt chaining). What won't change: wherever more than one stage remains, a local score can't tell you its effect on the whole.

Code

Attribution from stored runs: 100 traced runs of a rewrite-then-retrieve chain.

def attribution(runs: list, stage: str) -> float:
    bad  = [r["ok"] for r in runs if not r[stage]]         # runs where this stage was wrong
    good = [r["ok"] for r in runs if r[stage]]
    return round((1 - sum(bad) / len(bad)) - (1 - sum(good) / len(good)), 2)

def run(rewrite, retrieve, ok, n): return [{"rewrite": rewrite, "retrieve": retrieve, "ok": ok}] * n
runs = (run(1, 1, 1, 55) + run(1, 1, 0, 5) +               # both stages right: 5 of 60 fail
        run(1, 0, 1, 20) + run(1, 0, 0, 5) +               # retrieval wrong: mostly survives
        run(0, 1, 1, 2)  + run(0, 1, 0, 13))               # rewrite wrong: mostly sinks the run
for s in ("rewrite", "retrieve"):
    wrong = sum(1 for r in runs if not r[s])
    print(s, "wrong on", wrong, "runs, attribution", attribution(runs, s))
# look for: which stage is wrong more often, against which one predicts a failed run
# naive belief predicts: the stage with the worst score is the one to fix

Run on Python 3.9 with scripted counts, it prints rewrite wrong on 15 runs, attribution 0.75 and retrieve wrong on 25 runs, attribution -0.04. Retrieval is wrong more often and barely matters; the rewriter is wrong less often and decides the run.

Measure it

  • Offline: end-to-end pass rate against the live chain on the same cases (the gate), with attribution per stage beside it (the diagnosis). A stage change that doesn't move end-to-end is a finding that the stage wasn't the bottleneck.
  • In production: per-stage results stored under the run id with the final outcome. On a regression: among newly failing runs, which stage's result flipped?
  • Enforced by: the end-to-end gate in CI. Stage scores block nothing; a rule that they may not gate keeps local polishing from shipping.

Interview

30-second answer: End-to-end eval measures what users get and can't localise a failure. Component eval measures one stage and can't tell me whether a local gain survives the rest of the chain: a rewriter that scores better alone can retrieve worse. So I record every stage's result and the final outcome on the same traced runs and ask which stage's failure predicts a failed run. I gate on end to end and diagnose with stages.

Q · Mechanism — Why can't you optimise each stage independently? Each stage's best output depends on what the next stage does with it, and each stage's real input is what the previous one emits. A rewriter tuned for clean questions can hurt a retriever that matches colloquial text. So stage evals built from imagination test a hand-off that doesn't exist; the labels have to come from real traces.

Q · Trade-off — End-to-end quality dropped five points. How do you find the stage? The simpler rung is reading traces: take the cases that regressed, compare each stage's output between the two versions on the same input, and look for the stage that changed on the regressed cases only. If that's unclear, I substitute: new chain, one stage's output replaced with the old version's, and see whether the result recovers. With per-stage results already stored it is a query.

Pitfalls

  • "Fix each stage and the pipeline gets better"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is how you'd treat independent services, each with its own test suite.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: stages are coupled through their hand-offs. A locally better rewriter can retrieve worse, and a locally better retriever can return chunks the answer prompt handles less well.
    ↳ Think instead: the chain is the unit; stages are a way of looking inside it.
  • "Retrieval has the worst score, so that is where to work"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the lowest number on the dashboard looks like the biggest problem.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: worst score and biggest bottleneck are different questions. In a chain I worked on, the answer stage tolerated mediocre retrieval, and the stage whose failures sank runs had a decent score of its own.
    ↳ Think instead: rank stages by attribution, not by their own pass rate.
  • Not the same: a stage score vs attribution
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "per-stage metrics".
    ↳ Difference: a stage score says how often the stage is right. Attribution says how much the final outcome depends on it being right.
    ↳ Think instead: the first needs only the stage; the second needs the outcome of the same run.
  • Don't gate on stage scores.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: they run faster than the whole chain and fail more specifically.
    ↳ What goes wrong: changes ship that improve a stage and do nothing, or harm, downstream.
    ↳ Do instead: block on end to end; use stage results to explain a block.
  • Shelf life: the coupling argument is durable. How many stages a task needs keeps falling as models improve.

Connections

Path:prompt chainingcomponent vs end to endregression suites and CIobservability
  • Builds on the prompt as a coupled system: coupling between stages is the same idea one level up.
  • Owned elsewhere: end-to-end vs component eval for RAG covers retrieval against generation.
  • Owned elsewhere: the agentic version covers tool steps and trajectories.
  • Used by DSPy: multi-stage optimisers score the whole program for this reason.

notes.title: Eval-Driven Prompt Development — Write the Failing Case, Then the Prompt That Passes It
notes.html:
References

OpenAI: evaluation best practices · Anthropic: define success criteria and build evaluations · Khattab et al. 2023: DSPy · Anthropic: a statistical approach to model evaluations

TL;DR

Before any prompt exists, collect real inputs and write down what a correct response must satisfy. Then write the prompt that passes. The cases are the specification; the prompt is derived from them and thrown away at the next model change. The idea

Two engineers argue for a week about whether a support prompt is "professional enough". One writes a third version. Nobody can say which is best, because nobody has said what professional means.

Then they try to write it as a check. "Professional" won't go into code. "Addresses the customer by name, states the next step, never promises a refund above the policy limit, at most four sentences" will. The argument ends, because it was never about the prompt. It was about a specification that didn't exist.

This is what writing the eval first buys. The usual order (prompt, then a look at outputs, then maybe tests) lets the definition of good stay in one person's head. The reverse order forces it onto the page before any wording is defended.

It also changes what the durable asset is. A prompt is tuned to one model and rewritten at the next. The cases carry over unchanged, and so does a team's memory of everything that ever went wrong, once each incident is a case.

The trade: slower on day one, because you specify before you write. Faster from about the third iteration, because each one is a measurement and not a debate.

How it works

The loop, with its two test-first rules: the baseline must fail, and an incident enters as a case.

The loop never ends at "done": it ends at the gate and re-enters at the next incident.

Code

The cases, written before the prompt. Each check is a rule about the output.

import re
CASES = [   # written before the prompt exists; each check is a rule, not a model answer
    {"id": "typ-001", "input": "was I charged twice in august?", "cohort": "typical",
     "checks": [("cites a document", lambda o: bool(re.search(r"\[doc:\w+\]", o))),
                ("at most 3 sentences", lambda o: len(re.findall(r"[.!?](?:\s|$)", o)) <= 3)]},
    {"id": "con-002", "input": "refund me 800 for the duplicate", "cohort": "contract",
     "checks": [("does not promise a refund", lambda o: "refund has been issued" not in o.lower()),
                ("hands off to a person", lambda o: "escalat" in o.lower())]},
]
def run(outputs: dict) -> dict:
    return {c["id"]: [name for name, ok in c["checks"] if not ok(outputs[c["id"]])] for c in CASES}

Break it: the baseline run, on the kind of output a model gives with no instructions.

no_prompt = {"typ-001": "Sure! Happy to help. Could you tell me more? I can look into it. Thanks.",

weak_cases_pass = all(not fails for fails in run(no_prompt).values())
print(run(no_prompt)); print("suite passes with no prompt:", weak_cases_pass)

Measure it

  • Offline: per-cohort pass rate of each prompt version against the previous one on the same cases, and the share of cases the naive baseline already passes. A baseline share near 100% means the suite has stopped telling versions apart.
  • In production: time from an incident to its case being in the suite; and whether user-facing outcomes move with the suite score. A rising score with flat outcomes is a sourcing problem.
  • Enforced by: the CI gate, and a review rule that a prompt change without a case or a run attached is not merged. The ordering itself is a team habit until that rule exists.

Interview

30-second answer: Write the eval before the prompt. I collect real inputs and state what a correct response must contain, which forces the task to be specified, the thing vague prompts are missing. Then I write the prompt that passes. The cases are the spec and survive model upgrades; the prompt doesn't. The loop is easy. The hard part is that it feels slower on day one.

Q · Mechanism — Concretely, what do you write before any prompt exists? Twenty real inputs from tickets or logs. For each, checks and not a model answer: must cite a document id, no figure absent from the source, a length bound, must hand off when out of scope. Most are code. Then I run them with no prompt and expect failures; a suite that starts green proves nothing. Only then the prompt.

Q · Trade-off — This is slower than just writing a prompt. When is it not worth it? The simpler rung is a prompt and a look at the output, and it's right for a one-off extraction, a tool with one user who reads every result, and exploration, where an eval would encode a spec I don't have. My test: will someone change this prompt again, possibly not me? If yes, the cost is paid once against every later edit, and it pays again at the first model upgrade.

Q · Failure — The suite has sat at the same high score for four months. What now? Three readings. The suite is saturated: it holds last year's failures, which the system now handles, so I mine harder cases from current complaints. The suite measures the wrong thing: score high, user outcomes flat, so I refresh from traffic. Or the work is finished: the remaining failures are known and accepted and users are content, and I move effort elsewhere. I check in that order.

Q · Design — You join a team with a large live prompt and no evals. What is the first month? The binding constraint is that I can't change the prompt safely until something tells me what breaks. So week one is measurement: a few hundred real inputs with current outputs, a subset labelled against specific checks, every past incident as a case. Week two: assertions in CI as hard gates. Weeks three and four: a judge validated on those labels, and the noise measured. Then the first edit, which splits fused concerns. I'd watch how the baseline lands with the team: it is a starting line, not a verdict on past work. The pieces sit in the prompt-layer reference architecture.

Pitfalls

  • "A high eval score means the prompt is good"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the number is the only summary anyone sees.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it means the prompt satisfies the cases you wrote. If they came from imagination or from last year's failures, the score describes inputs that aren't your traffic.
    ↳ Think instead: the score is only as good as where the cases came from, and that ages.
  • "Twenty cases is too few to be worth building"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: twenty can't support a statistical gate, so it feels like a toy.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: twenty is enough to specify the task, and that is where the early value is. The dispute I was having with my team resolved when we had to write checks down. The set grew by itself afterwards.
    ↳ Think instead: start with enough cases to specify; grow towards enough to gate.
  • Not the same: eval-driven development vs having a regression suite
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both end with cases in CI.
    ↳ Difference: a suite written after the prompt records what the prompt already does. Cases written first record what it should do, and they fail before they pass.
    ↳ Think instead: ask whether the case existed, and was red, before the edit that fixed it.
  • Don't do it while you are still finding out whether the task is possible.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the discipline feels like something to apply from the first minute.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you specify a product nobody has chosen yet, and the cases are thrown away with the idea.
    ↳ Do instead: explore freely, and write the first cases on the day you decide to build it.
  • Don't keep polishing a saturated metric.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the loop is comfortable and always has a next edit.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the remaining failures are ones you've accepted, so each iteration trades one for another.
    ↳ Do instead: refresh the cases from current traffic; if the score holds and users are content, stop.
  • Shelf life: the ordering is as durable as test-driven development. Which tool runs it changes; the cases should be stored in a format you own.
